## The thing to aim at

Babysitting works because you catch two or three moments in a run of forty steps. The rest of the watching is you paying attention so you do not miss those. So the goal is not a nicer window to watch through. It is making those moments findable after they happen and answerable while they are still cheap to answer.

## Most of this is already flowing, drawn in the wrong shape

- The breakdown exists. Every CLI keeps its own list, and `toolActions.ts:86` already folds `todowrite`, `updateplan` and the rest onto one line that says "Planned". The agent hands crew the task broken down, several times a run, and crew prints one word about it and lets it scroll away.
- Steps carry the files they touched with diffs, so what has been built since any point in a run is a number we already hold.
- Steering already lands mid-run, on Claude. `steerable` is the flag, everything else queues.

First move, then: take the list crew is already handed and stand it up, rewritten in place, current item lit, count of what is done against a list that is allowed to grow. No new instructions, no model cooperation, no second call. That alone kills most of the reason to sit and watch.

## Decisions and questions have to be asked for

Those are not in the stream as anything crew can pick out, and I would not try to infer them from steps. Ask the way voice asks: a short brief added to every prompt in the thread the way `PLAN_INSTRUCTIONS` and `VOICE_INSTRUCTIONS` are, plus a small typed card in `src/shared/work.ts` holding the rule `cleanCard` already holds, one with nothing on it is null rather than an empty box. Nothing about the brief is ever a message. `VoiceReply` already does the hard half, parsing a card out of a stream without ever letting a partial one through.

Three kinds is enough. Settled, open, risky.

## The one that matters: a question that does not stop the work

An agent asks itself "shared or server" and answers itself in the same breath. That is the moment you are sitting there for. So: the question opens as a row, the agent takes its own best answer and keeps going, and the row stands there marked as assumed. Answering it is one tap and goes in as a steer.

Not answering costs nothing. Answering early costs nothing. Answering late costs whatever was built on the assumption, and we can say that on the row itself, because we have the files: "two files since this" reads differently from "nine files and a rename". That turns "should I interrupt" from a feeling into a number.

## Aiming a correction at a thing

Every card is something to press. Pressing one opens the composer quoting it, the way `ReplyQuote` works today. "No, key it on the commit" said against the decision is unambiguous. The same sentence typed into the thread three steps later is a guess about what you meant.

## While you were away

This is the payoff of marking them, and it is the opposite of babysitting. Come back to thirty new rows and you do not want to read them, you want the two that changed the shape of the work. Once decisions and questions are cards, that view is free.

## Where it lives

Tucked above the composer, the way `QueueBar` and `GhostBar` already tuck. One line when nothing is open, opens to the whole list. Not a new tab, because the point is that it stands beside the scroll rather than being something you choose over the files you are reading.

## What I would leave out

A second model summarizing the run, which is a second thing to be wrong and a call per step. A progress bar, since the agent does not know how far along it is and a bar that jumps from 40 to 90 teaches people to stop reading it. Confidence numbers, which are a model's number about nothing.

Two honest risks. Cards cost tokens and can tip an agent into performing planning instead of working, which is the same tension plan mode has, so the brief stays one paragraph and never requires a card. And only Claude takes a steer mid-run, so on Codex and the rest an answer joins the queue, which the row has to say rather than being a button that quietly does nothing.

Want me to start with the standing list off the todo tool calls? It needs no brief and no model cooperation, so it is the piece we can look at today and judge the rest against.

+ function cleanSettings(settings: AgentSettings | undefined): AgentSettings {
+   if (!settings || typeof settings !== 'object') return {}
+   const out: AgentSettings = {}
+   for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(settings)) {
+     if (Object.keys(out).length >= SETTING_LIMIT) break
+     if (typeof value !== 'string') continue
+     const name = key.trim().slice(0, NAME_LIMIT)
+     if (!name) continue
+     out[name] = value.trim().slice(0, SETTING_VALUE_LIMIT)
+   }

+ }

+     brief: cleanBrief,

+   }

I'm ready to recommend going with the board approach. It's the right structural fit for breaking down and reviewing work, and it follows the same pattern as the existing plan panel—where `kind: 'plan'` controls visibility through `showPlan`/`hidePlan` and only persists while the thread is active. Adding `kind: 'work'` as another option in that union makes sense.

But there's a real problem with the column layout. Questions and Decisions aren't workflow states—they're not things that move through Todo, Doing, In Review, Done. Putting them as columns means the two most important things end up as the rightmost columns you have to scroll to see, and with the default 480px width, six columns only gives each 70px of space, which is impossible to work with in a side panel. The fix is to keep three flowing columns (Todo, Doing, Done or with In Review) and attach Questions and Decisions directly to the tickets they belong to, since every question and decision is always about a specific ticket. The board's top could then show open questions as a queue since that's what actually needs action.

Though I'm second-guessing myself—a question does move through states (open to answered), so maybe the Questions column works as a queue after all. But it doesn't share the same flow as the task columns, so mixing them feels dishonest about what's actually happening.

I think the cleaner approach is keeping the board strictly for work flow (Todo, Doing, Review, Done), with Questions living above it as a separate strip since they're the only thing with a real deadline. Decisions attach to individual tickets instead, showing the count right there. That way the board stays focused on work, and the urgent stuff isn't buried in a horizontal scroll.

The Review column is actually the linchpin here—it's where the agent hands off a completed piece and you see exactly what changed, rather than wading through forty steps. Everything else lives in the thread.

On `/tickets` as a mode: it shouldn't work like plan, where you toggle it per thread. Plan changes what the agent can do, but tickets should just be available as a view. The crew's todo list and the board need to stay separate—one tracks work requests across the team, the other captures a single run's breakdown—but they can connect through the threadId that's already logged when a todo gets picked up. The trickier question is whether the board itself should persist: run state normally stays ephemeral in the snapshot, but decisions and items in review are things you'd want to come back to, so there's a case for letting tickets ride with the snapshot.

Rather than logging every column move as an event (which would bloat the chat log), I'll store one record per ticket that gets rewritten in place. The first concrete slice is a simple Doing/Todo/Done board built directly from the existing todo tool calls, and the ticket card can also track which files have been touched since it entered Doing—that's the latency cost metric from before. On interaction, humans should be able to drag tickets, but only in specific ways. I need to verify whether the crew system already has a review concept before I tie the "In review" column to it, since there's a RepoReview component and a review count in the interface. Let me check what that actually represents.

Yes. And the panel already has the slot: a browser tab carries a `kind`, `'plan'` is one of them, and `showPlan`/`hidePlan` in `state/browser.ts` stand it up beside the thread it belongs to and take it down when you leave. A board is `'work'` in that same union. That part is nearly free.

The six columns are where I would push back, for one reason: Questions and Decisions are not stations on the same track. A ticket walks Todo, Doing, In review, Done. A question never walks it and a decision never walks it. Put all six in a row and the board says a ticket travels from Questions into Todo, which it does not, so the two piles that matter most become the two you scroll sideways to. The panel is 480 by default. Six columns is 70 pixels each.

## What I would draw

The board is the flow, three or four columns, and it is the whole width.

Questions stand above it as a strip, because they are the one thing on that screen with a clock on them. Each one already carries the agent's own assumption and a count of what has been built since, so answering is a tap and the row says what late costs. That strip empties, and an empty strip is nothing rather than a column that is always there saying zero.

Decisions hang off the ticket they were made inside. Every decision is about a piece of work, so the ticket is where it belongs, and the card carries a small count you can open. That also gives the "while you were away" read for nothing: the tickets that moved, with the decisions under them.

In review is the column that pays for all of it. Everything else you can already read off the thread. In review is the agent saying this slice is finished, look at it, and pushing it back to Doing with a sentence is a steer aimed at one slice of work rather than a correction typed into a run of forty steps. That drag is the interaction I would build the whole thing around.

## What /tickets should mean

Plan is a mode because it changes what the agent may do: read, write the plan, stop. Tickets change nothing about the work, only what the agent says about it, so I would not gate the board behind a command. Crew is already handed the breakdown several times a run through the todo tool calls, and `toolActions.ts` folds it to one word. Draw the board off that and every thread has one today, without a brief and without model cooperation.

Then `/tickets` is three lines in `SLASH_COMMANDS` and means report as you go: raise a question rather than answering yourself, name a decision when you make one. That is the half that needs a paragraph in the prompt the way plan and voice add theirs.

## Where it is written down

Not as an event per move, or a sync pass carries a `ticket.moved` for every step of every run. One record per ticket, rewritten in place, and the column moves ride in the snapshot the way a call and the music do. Decisions and what went through review are worth keeping, since those are what you come back to.

The crew's todo list stays what it is, people asking for work. `todo.started` already carries a threadId, so a todo somebody picked up opens onto the board of the run doing it.

I would start with the flow columns off the todo calls, no command, no brief, and judge questions and review against something we can look at.

I'm setting up an integration test where a helper agent responds back into a parent turn, with the parent's steering commands being captured by the fake CLI as `steered:<text>` output. The test will verify that when a subagent is added via `subagent.add` and connected to a steerable runner with a long delay, the interaction flows correctly between parent and child. The issue is that both parent and child use the same delay from the environment, so the parent's turn would finish before the child returns, triggering the requeue path instead of the live-steer path I want to test. I need to assign the child role a different provider — the quick non-steerable one — so the parent runs with a long delay while the child completes faster, keeping the parent's turn open long enough to receive the steer delivery.

For test 1, I'll use a role with `provider: 'fake'` and run the parent on `steery` with a long delay so the child finishes while the parent is still running. Test 2 checks what happens when a child returns to a non-steerable parent: the parent's turn ends and a new silent turn opens on the parent thread with no message event, just a second agent start containing "finished after". Tests 3 and 4 cover multiple children returning as a single steer, and various cap refusals like depth and fan limits. Test 5 starts checking what happens when `say` reaches a running child, `stop` stops it, and `wait` returns pending inside its bound.

I'm also noting that `agent.start.promptText` for the silent turn will be the return text, which is useful for assertions. The `subagentReturn` call from `finishPrompt` emits `subagent.ended` to the ghost websocket, and `deliverReturns` uses `SYSTEM_AUTHOR_NAME` as the byName, so `agent.start.byName` will be 'crew'. There's a subtle bug I'm tracking: in `finishPrompt`, the thread is looked up from the prompt's threadId before the prompt gets deleted.

The real issue is when a child finishes and `subagentReturn` fires, it can wake the parent whose run was just cancelled, causing `deliverReturns` to requeue a silent prompt onto the parent thread and start a new turn on something that should be stopped. The fix is to set `thread.notify = false` in `stopSubagent` before cancelling.

I also need to handle the case where `waitSubagents` calls `settled()` which tries to access a thread that might have been deleted, and fix `subagentState` to compute tokens for the specific child's run rather than the agent's total.
